title: The Chain From Seed to Shelf

pages.text: Madam Yartey gave each pupil a card on a string. “Today we play the chain from farm to table,” she said. Sumaiya’s card said farmer. Wumpini’s said processor. Others said input dealer, transporter, packer, shopkeeper and customer. Three more cards said extension officer, savings group and cooperative. “Every link has costs and risks,” said Madam Yartey. “Nobody in the chain is a villain, and nobody works for free.”

pages.alt: A teacher hands out role cards on strings to pupils in a line at the front of a classroom.

pages.text: The chain began with cassava. Sumaiya grew it and sold a bag to Wumpini. “Suppose I sell it for one hundred cedis,” she said. Wumpini peeled, grated, pressed and roasted it into gari. He packed it in clean bags, and the shopkeeper sold the bags. “Suppose the shop sells the gari from that cassava for two hundred and fifty cedis,” said Madam Yartey. “These are imaginary numbers. The difference pays for work, fuel, transport, packaging, rent and risk. It is not all profit.”

pages.text: “Where is value added?” asked Madam Yartey. The pupils named steps: grading, drying, processing, packaging, storing and transporting. “Value addition,” she said, “means making a product worth more by improving it. Storing can also add value. The grain study we read found that selling straight after harvest was linked to a loss of about twenty-nine per cent of sales value, because prices rise later. But storing needs a good bag or store, and money to wait.”

pages.text: “Now a story from Rwanda,” said Madam Yartey. “Coffee farmers there once sold their coffee cherries to traders. In 2000, aid-funded projects helped build coffee washing stations and organise farmers into cooperatives. Farmers and tasters were trained in quality. According to a trade article, about twenty-seven per cent of Rwanda’s coffee exports are now specialty coffee, up from almost none in 2000, and it sells for fifteen to twenty-five per cent above market prices. One cooperative manager says his income is about five times what it was before 2001. That is his own account.”

pages.alt: A teacher points to Rwanda on a map beside a drawing of coffee cherries and a washing station.

pages.text: “What made it work?” asked Madam Yartey. Sumaiya answered: “Shared washing stations, quality rules, training and cooperatives.” “One farmer cannot afford a washing station,” said the teacher, “but a cooperative can. It also had traceability, which means buyers can see where the coffee came from. But the project started with aid money, and success in one country does not guarantee it in another. Also, the article is not new, so the figures may have changed.”

pages.alt: A teacher draws a washing station shared by many small farms with a label saying traceable.

pages.text: The class turned to Ghana. “Choose one crop in our district,” said Madam Yartey. They picked tomatoes. They drew the chain, marked where tomatoes spoil, and asked: who could add value? Sumaiya suggested grading and clean crates. Wumpini suggested drying or making paste, if a market and clean water could be found. Another pupil suggested a shared cold room or a group selling arrangement. “Choose only one small step,” said Madam Yartey, “and find out what it needs: power, roads, buyers, money and rules.”

pages.text: Madam Yartey asked for a summary of forty-five words or fewer. Sumaiya wrote: “A farm-to-market chain has many links, each with costs and risks. Value grows through grading, drying, processing and packaging. Rwanda’s coffee farmers raised quality and earnings by sharing washing stations in cooperatives. Ghanaian farmers could start by choosing one link to improve together.” Wumpini counted the words aloud. “Forty-three,” he said. “Within the limit.”

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: to write a summary, read the passage twice, underline the main points, leave out examples and figures that are not needed, use your own words, join the points in one paragraph, and count your words. Sumaiya used linking ideas and no contractions or slang. A summary must be accurate: it should never add a fact that the passage does not give. The end.
